main_message: Steel power has always been about controlling the 'path' from raw material to market. Carnegie bought it, governments now gatekeep it with tariffs and a golden share, and the EU is putting a carbon toll on it. America's share fell because the world grew, not because US output collapsed.
why_hook: The paradox of the same tonnage at half the share versus 4 percent is a good puzzle, and the 'guarded like a weapon' line adds stakes. But the 'nearly as much' phrasing is clumsy: it reads as a contradiction before the numbers are explained.
what_connects_layers: The 'who controls the path' frame works rhetorically and ties Carnegie, Section 232 and the golden share, and CBAM together. The third layer is the weakest link. A carbon price is a cost on emissions, not control of a physical path, so it stretches the metaphor. The 71 vs 11 percent EAF setup is good, but the hydrogen segment drifts.
ending_comment: It answers with 'share and control of the path, not tonnage', which resolves the opening paradox. It then honestly declines to judge whether the cost is worth it. The Edgar Thomson closing image is strong, though 'still makes steel today' needs to be exactly right.

boring_or_slow.why: A dense stack of OECD numbers (capacity, gap, exports, subsidy multiples) plus EU quota figures with no breathing room.
Long deal chronology with many dates (Biden block, Trump order, closing five days later), then the golden share details.
The CBAM mechanics (50-tonne threshold, certificate timing, free allocation, deductions) plus the illustrative calculation are heavy to follow by ear.
A hedged, inconclusive segment (HYBRIT, then Stegra 'timeline under review') that adds little to the argument.

confusing.quote: it made nearly as much — and that was about four percent
confusing.why: The sentence is ambiguous on first hearing. 'Nearly as much' of what? Tonnage or share? It only resolves later.

confusing.quote: roughly half of all the steel made on Earth that year
confusing.why: 1944 at 81 Mt and 1950 at 88 Mt followed by 'still close to half' is fine, but the wartime peak versus the 1950 comparison is easy to lose by ear.

confusing.quote: eighty-eight million tonnes in 1950, and about eighty-two million in 2025
confusing.why: Fewer tonnes in 2025 than in 1950, yet 'roughly the same' and 'nearly as much'. The intro said 'nearly as much', which glosses over a decline of about 7 percent. Also 88/189 is about 47 percent, so 'almost half' holds, but the arithmetic is left to the viewer.

confusing.quote: Importers bringing more than fifty tonnes
confusing.why: The exemption threshold (de minimis) is mentioned without saying it exempts small importers, and the free-allocation adjustment is dropped into the middle of the explanation.

confusing.quote: Steel made with less of it faces a smaller charge
confusing.why: The 'path' metaphor is stretched here. A carbon charge is not control of a route.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: a man Carnegie described as having started out as a poor railway clerk
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Carnegie's autobiography is the main source for his own story, so the Frick portrayal and the rise-from-nothing framing come from him. Homestead is covered, but through a dry state marker, with little on Frick's role, wages, or the broken union.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.direction: Slightly toward the administration's framing, then balanced by CRS
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Utilization of 77 percent against an 80 percent target is presented even-handedly, but the downstream costs of the tariffs (steel-using industries, jobs, prices) get one sentence. The video is thin on the economics of the cost side.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: China's steel exports alone were larger than everything the United States produced
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: The OECD overcapacity and subsidy framing is presented as fact. Missing: that much Chinese export is driven by domestic property-sector collapse, and that Chinese steel is a global commodity with buyers who benefit.

claims_you_doubt.quote: In 1950, America made almost half of the world's steel. In 2025, it made nearly as much
claims_you_doubt.why: 'Nearly as much' is loose. 88 Mt vs 82 Mt is a roughly 7 percent drop, and the intro hides it. Worse, the early 1950s share was inflated by a devastated Europe and Japan, which the video never says.

claims_you_doubt.quote: roughly half of all the steel made on Earth that year
claims_you_doubt.why: 1944 is a plausible figure, but this is a wartime peak with the Axis economies also producing, and the world total is partly reconstructed. It needs a caveat or a firmer source.

Carnegie's famous line is real, but it comes from later years, not the 1870s rail price of about $70 a ton just before. Putting them back to back implies a continuous price story without saying decades passed.

claims_you_doubt.quote: Economists call this vertical integration: own each step, so nobody can charge you for theirs
claims_you_doubt.why: This is a simplification. Vertical integration is also about reducing transaction costs and supply risk, and the mid-1880s Frick buy-in is described as 'half the stock'. The details are plausible but not checkable from the script alone.

claims_you_doubt.quote: not mainly because American output collapsed
claims_you_doubt.why: True in aggregate, but the US output actually peaked in the 1970s, fell sharply in the 1980s, and in the integrated-mill sector there was a real collapse (Youngstown, Pittsburgh, Bethlehem). The video skips the deindustrialization story entirely and reads as if nothing painful happened, which a steel-industry viewer will find glib.

claims_you_doubt.quote: from about seventy-two percent in 2017 to about seventy-seven percent
claims_you_doubt.why: Capacity utilization is heavily affected by the 2020 COVID dip and recovery, and by changes in the capacity denominator. Attributing the move to tariffs is shaky, which is why the CRS mixed-effects line matters; the video should say more.

claims_you_doubt.quote: The Edgar Thomson works... still makes steel today
claims_you_doubt.why: Factually true (it is part of US Steel's Mon Valley Works), but it is named from the 1870s and the plant has been rebuilt many times. Also, the claim of a 'veto' overstates the golden share: it is consent rights over specified decisions, which the video itself defined more narrowly in segment 9.

best_moment: 09 — It takes the popular 'government now owns U.S. Steel' claim, tests it against the companies' own announcement, and shows the real, narrower powers, then ties it back to Carnegie's path.
top3_fixes: Fix the opening so the paradox is unambiguous: say 'about 88 million tonnes in 1950, about 82 million in 2025 — but that went from almost half the world to four percent.' Drop 'nearly as much', and add one line on why 1950 was inflated (Europe and Japan in ruins).

Add the missing middle: the 1970s-80s collapse of integrated mills (Youngstown, Bethlehem), the rise of minimills and imports, and the human cost. Otherwise 'America didn't stop making steel' reads as glib to anyone who knows the industry, and the Homestead dryness is mirrored by silence on later job losses.

Cut or merge segments 08 and 11 and simplify the CBAM mechanics. Keep one or two OECD numbers, drop the hydrogen hedging, and say plainly that the 'path' metaphor stretches for carbon: a toll on emissions, not control of a route. Also reword the closing 'veto' to match the narrower golden-share powers in 09.
